label: Merge
description: Written after a period of financial and creative doubt, this album turns Taylor's worries into some of his most direct, tuneful songwriting, backed by a road-tested band playing loose, breezy country-soul. Horns and pedal steel color songs about work, fatherhood, and getting by. It is often cited as the emotional center of his Merge run.
lineage: Continues the Dead- and Band-inflected country-rock direction set on Lateness of Dancers, cementing Hiss Golden Messenger as a hub of the 2010s cosmic-country revival.
key_tracks: Like a Mirror Loves a Hammer

label: Merge
description: A quick, joyful counterpart to Heart Like a Levee's worry, recorded fast with the touring band and leaning into gospel-tinged uplift. The guitars are warmer and more interlocked than on earlier records, with less studio polish and more live-in-the-room feel. Taylor has described it as a record about gratitude in hard times.
lineage: Keeps Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic-country sound loose and communal, closer to the Dead's road-band ethos than the more arranged Heart Like a Levee.

label: Merge
description: A more expansive, guest-heavy record featuring Aaron Dessner, John James Tourville, and Buddy Miller, stretching Hiss Golden Messenger's country-soul into longer, more atmospheric arrangements. Themes of self-doubt and endurance run through the lyrics, delivered over some of the band's most layered playing to date. It was recorded partly at Dessner's Long Pond studio.
lineage: Expands the Merge-era cosmic-country sound with outside collaborators, tying Hiss Golden Messenger to the wider 2010s indie-Americana network around Bon Iver and the National.

label: Merge
description: Written and largely recorded in isolation during 2020, this record folds subtle synths and drum machine textures into Hiss Golden Messenger's usual country-soul, without losing the pedal steel and warm harmonies. The songs reckon with pandemic-era stillness and small-town North Carolina life in equal measure. It is a quieter, more reflective entry than its predecessors.
lineage: Shows Taylor bending his Dead- and Band-rooted sound toward home-studio textures while keeping the same cosmic-country core.
key_tracks: Way Back in the Way Back
If It Comes in the Morning

label: Merge
description: A relatively lean, upbeat record that returns to full-band arrangements after the home-recorded Quietly Blowing It, with brighter tempos and some of Taylor's most direct choruses. Pedal steel and harmony vocals sit up front, in keeping with the buttery, breezy sound that defines his Merge catalog. It arrived as Taylor marked over a decade of recording as Hiss Golden Messenger.
lineage: A late-period return to the communal, road-band version of Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic country after a more solitary pandemic record.

label: Mexican Summer
description: Williamson's Mexican Summer debut sets her plainspoken, drawling voice against loose, twangy full-band arrangements, a step up in scale from her earlier home-recorded albums. Songs move between hushed acoustic passages and warmer country-rock breeze, dealing frankly with sex, loneliness, and desert landscapes. It established her as part of the label's cosmic-leaning Americana roster.
lineage: Moves Williamson's earlier lo-fi folk toward a fuller Laurel Canyon-indebted country-rock sound, setting up her later work as one half of Plains with Katie Crutchfield.

label: Mexican Summer
description: A patient, spacious record built around Williamson's low, unhurried voice and finger-picked and pedal-steel-laced arrangements, recorded partly at Sonic Ranch in Texas. It trades the rawer edges of Cosmic Wink for a smoother, more mystical take on desert country-rock. Themes of self-possession and desire run through its longer, breezier songs.
lineage: Continues Williamson's Mexican Summer-era cosmic country lineage, deepening the Parsons- and Laurel Canyon-indebted sound she'd carry into her Plains collaboration.

label: Mexican Summer
description: Recorded in Marfa and Nashville after Williamson's move back to Texas, this album is her most fully country-identified record, with pedal steel, warm harmonies, and road-song imagery throughout. It processes a broken engagement with a directness that critics linked to both Lucinda Williams and classic outlaw country. It marked her strongest crossover into the wider Americana conversation.
lineage: Brings Williamson's cosmic-country sound closest to its Gram Parsons and outlaw-country roots, continuing the lineage she shares with Plains partner Katie Crutchfield.

label: Jagjaguwar
description: Max Clarke's first full-length as Cut Worms leans on ringing, Everly Brothers-style harmonies and simple, twangy guitar figures played at an unhurried country-pop tempo. It is a warm, sunny record that wears its 1960s and '70s country-rock influences openly without pastiche. Clarke's plainspoken songwriting keeps the mood breezy even when the lyrics turn wistful.
lineage: Draws directly on Gram Parsons-style country-rock and Laurel Canyon harmony singing, filtered through a Brooklyn DIY-pop sensibility.

label: Jagjaguwar
description: A double album that widens Cut Worms' sound with brighter production, horns, and more layered harmonies while keeping the same easy country-pop tempos. Clarke's songwriting stays plain and melodic, closer to classic AM radio than to twang-rock swagger. It is the most expansive record in his catalog.
lineage: Extends the buttery, harmony-driven Laurel Canyon and Everly Brothers lineage of Hollow Ground into a longer, more varied set.

label: Jagjaguwar
description: The self-titled third album pares Cut Worms' sound back to a leaner, more direct country-pop, recorded with a full band after Clarke relocated from New York to Los Angeles. Melodies stay bright and hooky, riding on the same twangy, harmony-laden guitar interplay as his earlier work. It reads as a mid-career consolidation rather than a reinvention.
lineage: Keeps Cut Worms anchored in the Parsons/Everly Brothers country-pop lineage that runs through his whole catalog.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Written after Morby found an old photograph of his father presumed near-death, this album is a warm, mid-tempo meditation on mortality and memory, built on breezy country-rock arrangements with pedal steel and horns. Recorded partly in Memphis, it draws on that city's soul and gospel history as much as on Laurel Canyon songwriting. Josh Terry has called it Morby's best record.
lineage: Continues Morby's move toward a fuller, Dead- and Band-inflected cosmic country sound, and set up the piano-based sessions of More Photographs.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Morby's latest album spreads thirteen songs across a bucolic, folk-rock palette, continuing the warm, unhurried style of This Is a Photograph with an even more pastoral, near-spiritual tone. Pedal steel and acoustic textures dominate over the breezy tempos. Terry named it among his favorites of the year it appeared.
lineage: Extends Morby's Dead Oceans-era cosmic country songwriting, keeping him a central figure of the 2020s Americana-indie crossover.

label: ANTI-
description: A more exploratory record than Mangy Love, stretching several songs into long, Dead-like instrumental passages built on interlocking guitar lines. McCombs' deadpan, riddling lyrics stay intact even as the band jams out around them. Critics singled out its patient, cosmic-rock second half as some of his most ambitious playing.
lineage: Leans furthest into the Grateful Dead-style long-form guitar jam of any McCombs record, tying him directly to the Cosmic American Music revival.

label: Sacred Bones
description: Damon McMahon's breakthrough as Amen Dunes trades his earlier lo-fi murk for warmer, more melodic songs built on loping acoustic guitar and a breathy, drawling voice. Tempos stay slow and breezy, closer to hazy folk-rock than to the drone of his debut. It is the record that widened his audience beyond the noise-folk underground.
lineage: Moves Amen Dunes toward a hazier, Dead- and Parsons-adjacent guitar-folk sound documented in his own account of listening to classic rock while writing it.

label: Sacred Bones
description: A more polished, radio-scaled record than Love, mixing McMahon's drawled vocals with warmer production, occasional synths, and mid-tempo grooves that borrow as much from classic rock as from psych-folk. Songs draw obliquely on McMahon's own family history and the pressures of masculinity. It became his most widely reviewed album to date.
lineage: Extends the breezy, classic-rock-informed direction of Love into a fuller studio sound, keeping Amen Dunes tied to the wider Cosmic American Music-adjacent revival.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Cohen's solo debut after Deerhoof and the Curtains sets warped, subdued psychedelic pop against loose, home-recorded arrangements. Guitars ring and drift rather than solo, and the tempos stay unhurried throughout. It established the mysterious, hazy sound that runs through his later solo work.
lineage: Draws on Laurel Canyon-style breezy pop songwriting filtered through a lo-fi, tape-warped production sensibility.

label: Captured Tracks
description: A slightly warmer, more melodic follow-up to Overgrown Path, keeping Cohen's soft-focus psychedelic pop but adding more overt hooks and clearer vocal lines. Tempos remain breezy and the mood mellow throughout. It continues his run of quietly beloved, low-key solo records.
lineage: Refines the hazy, Laurel Canyon-adjacent pop songwriting of Overgrown Path without changing course.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Cohen's self-titled third album keeps his mumbled, half-buried vocal style but opens the arrangements up with more keyboard and synth color. The tempos stay slow and breezy, and the mood remains warm rather than melancholy. It is generally regarded as the most fully realized record in his solo catalog.
lineage: Continues Cohen's subdued psychedelic-pop lineage, indebted to Laurel Canyon songwriting as much as to his own art-pop background in Deerhoof.

label: Bella Union
description: Wilson's breakout solo debut is a sprawling, hour-long homage to Laurel Canyon songwriting, built on layered acoustic and pedal-steel textures and long, patient guitar passages. Recorded in his own Laurel Canyon studio with guests including members of Wilco and Dawes, it directly revives the Crosby, Stills & Nash and Neil Young sound of the neighborhood's golden age. It made Wilson a central figure of the 2010s cosmic-country and folk-rock revival.
lineage: A conscious, documented recreation of the Laurel Canyon country-rock sound of Gram Parsons and CSNY, made in the same physical neighborhood that produced it.

label: Bella Union
description: A denser, more orchestrated follow-up to Gentle Spirit, adding strings and a wider cast of guests (including David Crosby and Graham Nash) to Wilson's long-form country-rock songs. Extended guitar jams and layered harmonies stretch several tracks well past the six-minute mark. It further cemented Wilson's reputation as a producer-auteur of the Laurel Canyon revival.
lineage: Expands Gentle Spirit's Laurel Canyon and Grateful Dead-indebted guitar-rock into a more maximalist, string-laden record.

label: Bella Union
description: A more synth-laced, polished record than Wilson's first two albums, though still built around long, winding guitar solos and breezy tempos. It reflects his work as a Roger Waters sideman and in-demand producer during this period, with a slicker, more 1980s-tinged studio sound. Fans of his earlier folk-rock leaned mixed, but the guitar-forward core remained.
lineage: Shows Wilson's Laurel Canyon revivalism absorbing more polished, synth-rock textures without abandoning its long-solo, cosmic foundation.

label: BMG
description: Recorded in Nashville with a crew of bluegrass and session players, this album pulls Wilson's sound closest to straight country, adding fiddle and pedal steel to his usual breezy, long-form guitar writing. It is a warmer, more rootsy record than Rare Birds, closer in spirit to Gentle Spirit. Wilson has described it as a return to more direct songwriting.
lineage: Brings Wilson's Laurel Canyon revivalism back toward its country-rock and Gram Parsons roots by way of Nashville session musicians.

label: American Recordings
description: Ethan Miller's band follows up their debut with a bigger, Rick Rubin-produced record of heavy, extended guitar jams built on Crazy Horse-style fuzz and Southern-rock swagger. Songs stretch out into long instrumental sections without losing their anthemic hooks. It is generally considered Howlin Rain's breakthrough.
lineage: A direct continuation of the Neil Young & Crazy Horse and Allman Brothers long-jam lineage, filtered through Miller's earlier work in the psych band Comets on Fire.
key_tracks: Dancers at the End of Time

label: American Recordings
description: A dense, heavily produced record of sprawling, riff-driven rock songs, several stretching past seven minutes with extended guitar interplay. It leans harder into arena-scaled classic rock than Howlin Rain's earlier records, while keeping the same Dead- and Crazy Horse-indebted jam structure. Miller has called it the most difficult record he made with the band.
lineage: Pushes the Crazy Horse and Southern-rock long-jam lineage of Magnificent Fiend toward a heavier, more maximalist studio sound.

label: Silver Current Records
description: A looser, more organic-sounding record than The Russian Wilds, recorded live off the floor with a new lineup and leaning into warmer, more soulful arrangements. Extended guitar solos still anchor several songs, but the overall feel is breezier and less studio-heavy. It marked Miller's move to his own Silver Current label.
lineage: Returns Howlin Rain's Crazy Horse-and-Dead-indebted jamming to a rawer, band-in-a-room sound after the maximalism of The Russian Wilds.

label: Silver Current Records
description: A double album that stretches Howlin Rain's long-form jamming even further, with several tracks built around extended, exploratory guitar sections in the mode of the Dead's live improvisation. It is the most explicitly psychedelic and least song-oriented record in Miller's catalog. Fans of the band's jam-rock side consider it a high point.
lineage: The fullest expression of Howlin Rain's Grateful Dead- and Crazy Horse-style extended-jam songwriting.

label: Single Lock Records
description: A more textured, golden-toned record than Putting On Airs, layering Rae's strong, unhurried voice over AM-radio-indebted arrangements that Terry called never kitschy despite the vintage flourishes. Every arrangement stays tasteful and uncluttered, in keeping with the breezy Cosmic American Music lineage she works in. It builds on her Single Lock catalog without repeating it.
lineage: Extends Rae's Nashville country-folk lineage, tying her to the same Single Lock circle of Muscle Shoals-adjacent Americana artists.

label: Drag City
description: Hanson's first solo album away from his fuzzed-out band Wand strips things back to gentle, string-and-pedal-steel-laced folk-rock, closer to Gene Clark than to Wand's noise. His high, plaintive voice sits up front over patient, breezy arrangements. It is a quiet detour from the guitar heroics of his main band.
lineage: Moves Hanson from Wand's psych-fuzz toward a hushed, Laurel Canyon-adjacent country-folk sound that resurfaces in his later solo work.

label: Drag City
description: A fuller-band, more overtly country-rock record than Hanson's debut, with pedal steel and long, winding guitar solos running through desert-toned songs. It leans into the sound of vintage Neil Young and Gene Clark records without straight pastiche. Critics noted it as his most cohesive solo statement to date.
lineage: Pulls Hanson's solo work closer to classic Cosmic American Music, sitting alongside labelmates like Bill Callahan on Drag City's roster.

label: Drag City
description: A provocatively titled record built around ten-minute guitar-solo epics, closer to Hanson's Wand side than his quieter solo debut. Country-rock tempos and pedal steel still anchor the songs even as the guitar playing stretches out at length. Terry called it instantly likable despite the sprawl.
lineage: Reconnects Hanson's solo work to the long-form, Dead- and Crazy Horse-style guitar jamming of the Cosmic American Music lineage.

label: Drag City
description: A full swerve from Hanson's scorching guitar-rock records into piano-led, orchestral Nashville Sound balladry, as Josh Terry described it, with sarcastic, well-built songs. It keeps the breezy tempos of his earlier work while trading long solos for lusher, more classic-country arrangement. It is his most stylistically surprising solo record.
lineage: Bends Hanson's Cosmic American Music-indebted solo catalog toward classic Nashville Sound orchestration.

label: New West Records
description: Produced by Jeff Tweedy, this album pairs the Saskatchewan cousins' antique folk repertoire and close harmonies with warmer, more electric backing than their earlier records, edging toward a breezy country-rock feel. Clayton Linthicum's fingerpicked and occasionally fuzzed guitar work sits alongside Kacy Anderson's plain, unadorned voice. It was their first release for a US label.
lineage: Bridges Kacy & Clayton's traditional Canadian folk repertoire with the Laurel Canyon-adjacent country-rock arrangements Tweedy brought to the sessions.

label: New West Records
description: A fuller-band record than The Siren's Song, with more electric guitar interplay and a breezier tempo, while keeping the duo's plainspoken, old-timey vocal delivery. Produced again with outside help, it leans further from strict folk revivalism toward a country-rock sound. It continued their run on New West alongside labelmates working similar traditionalist-to-rock territory.
lineage: Extends Kacy & Clayton's move from pure folk repertoire toward a Laurel Canyon-style country-rock sound.

label: Self-released
description: A tighter, more song-focused record than Cosmic Cash, though still anchored by extended guitar interplay between the band's two lead players. Tempos loosen into breezier, more melodic territory in places, without giving up the long jams entirely. It shows the band refining rather than abandoning their Dead-indebted approach.
lineage: Continues Garcia Peoples' Grateful Dead-inspired dual-guitar jamming within the same New Jersey/New York psych-rock underground as Endless Boogie and Woods.

label: Self-released
description: The debut LP from Angie Willcutt and Micah Wu (of Artificial Go and ROD) is eight brief, folk-based songs built on plucked strings and a mallet-driven pulse, released on Willcutt's own imprint. Willcutt's playful, transcendental lyrics float over Wu's spare, exploratory arrangements. Josh Terry called it spectral, cosmic folk-pop that is somewhat spooky despite its short 23-minute runtime.
lineage: A hushed, folk-song take on Cosmic American Music by two members of a more frantic Los Angeles band, closer to Vashti Bunyan than to full-band jam-rock.

label: Self-released
description: The debut full-length from Chicago duo Joshua Condon and Eliza Weber, following a decade of self-released EPs, sets warm harmony vocals against loose, breezy guitar arrangements. The songs move at an easy tempo somewhere between cosmic country and dream-pop. It was the first Glyders record to reach a wider audience beyond Chicago clubs.
lineage: A slow-building DIY project that channels Laurel Canyon-style harmony songwriting through a decade of Chicago house-show self-release culture.

label: Full Time Hobby
description: A Nashville collective built around players who also work in Shrunken Elvis and Rich Ruth's band, this self-titled record blends Radiohead-style atmospherics with Nilsson-esque psychedelic pop and woozy, pub-rock-adjacent Americana. Josh Terry linked its ties to Nashville's Rich Ruth and Shrunken Elvis scene of instrumentalists reworking country and soul textures. It marked the project's debut on the UK label Full Time Hobby.
lineage: Extends Nashville's instrumentalist-led cosmic country scene (Shrunken Elvis, Rich Ruth, Spencer Cullum) into a more song-based, psychedelic-pop direction.

label: Woodsist
description: Andrews (a longtime member of the Woods/Woodsist scene, formerly of Quilt) leads this loose, sunny record of ramshackle country-folk, recorded at his farmhouse in the Hudson Valley. Ringing guitars and easygoing tempos carry conversational, unfussy songwriting throughout. It sits comfortably alongside labelmate Woods in the Woodsist roster's twangy, DIY take on Laurel Canyon songwriting.
lineage: Continues the Woodsist label's lineage of hazy, harmony-driven country-folk that runs through Woods and Cut Worms as well.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Adam Granduciel's full-length debut with the band, a hazy blend of Dylan-style harmonica and drawl with Crazy Horse guitar sprawl. Long, meandering tracks like 'Buenos Aires Beach' stretch toward Americana psychedelia rather than pop songcraft. It is for listeners who want the roots of the band's later widescreen sound in a rawer, more ragged form.
lineage: Grew out of Granduciel and Kurt Vile's shared Philadelphia scene and Dylan/Neil Young influences, feeding directly into the more polished cosmic-Americana of the band's later records.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: The War on Drugs' second album layers motorik drum-machine pulse under harmonica, slide guitar and reverb-soaked vocals, moving toward the widescreen sound the band would perfect later. Tracks bleed into one another like a long highway drive, closer to Springsteen-via-Eno than jam-band twang. A transitional record between the group's scrappier debut and its arena-ready future.
lineage: Bridges the band's Crazy Horse-inflected debut and the fully-formed synth-Americana of Lost in the Dream, with Kurt Vile's departure from the lineup shaping its more singular vision.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: The band's breakthrough: widescreen, synth-lined heartland rock with long, patient builds, pedal-steel-like guitar figures and Granduciel's plainspoken, hurting voice. As Josh Terry put it in a Wild Pink interview, this record 'clicked' for a generation of songwriters discovering their own voice. It is the album that made cosmic Americana a viable indie-rock lane again.
lineage: Descended from Dylan, Petty and Springsteen filtered through Eno-style production, and became a direct influence on artists like Wild Pink and Hovvdy.

label: Atlantic
description: The band's major-label debut pushes the sound even more polished and arena-scaled, with layered guitars, synth pads and a Grammy-winning sheen. It trades some of the earlier records' ragged charm for widescreen consistency, still built on long-form, slow-building songs. A record for driving at night with the windows down.
lineage: Extends the cosmic-Americana approach of Lost in the Dream into a more maximalist, radio-scaled register.

label: Woodsist
description: Jeremy Earl's Brooklyn band moves from bedroom-folk haze to a full-band, live-sounding record with the addition of Jarvis Taveniere and G. Lucas Crane's cassette collages. Earl's falsetto floats over fuzzy, Crazy Horse-style guitar runs and Kraut-rock-tinged jams. A defining record of the late-2000s Woodsist/DIY scene.
lineage: Grew out of Earl's early lo-fi cassette recordings; established the template of sunny psych-folk and extended guitar jams that fed the label's roster (Real Estate, White Fence, Kurt Vile).

label: Woodsist
description: The follow-up to Songs of Shame leans further into sun-soaked pop hooks while keeping the tape-hiss production and Earl's high, reedy voice. Long instrumental passages and Crane's found-sound collage keep it from ever feeling too straightforward. A quintessential entry in the Woodsist label's back catalog.
lineage: Continues directly from Songs of Shame's template of Crazy Horse guitar sprawl and DIY tape production.

label: Woodsist
description: Woods stretch out further here, with side-long instrumental jams sitting next to their usual sun-dappled pop songs. It is the most explicitly Dead-indebted record in their catalog to that point, trading some of the earlier tape-hiss murk for cleaner, more expansive guitar interplay.
lineage: Marks the band's turn toward longer, more overtly jam-based arrangements, anticipating Bend Beyond and the band's live reputation.

label: Woodsist
description: Recorded upstate with a more deliberate, less improvisatory process than past records, Bend Beyond captures the muscular, Crazy Horse-inflected live show the band had built over years of touring. The title track is an extended showcase for the group's guitar interplay. A high point of the band's Woodsist-era run.
lineage: The culmination of the band's 2009-2012 Woodsist run, after which they continued to evolve toward more polished psych-pop on later albums.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Ripley Johnson's (Wooden Shjips, Moon Duo) country-rock solo project debuts with seven warm, unhurried songs built on layered acoustic and electric guitars and Barry Walker's pedal steel. It trades Wooden Shjips' krautrock drone for direct, breezy homage to 1970s private-press country rock.
lineage: Grew directly out of Johnson's psych-rock work in Wooden Shjips and Moon Duo, redirected toward Gram Parsons/Grateful Dead-style country rock; became a flagship of the 2020s cosmic-country revival.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: The second Rose City Band album widens the sound with fuller arrangements and a sunnier, more anthemic set of songs, still anchored by Johnson's laconic voice and Barry Walker's pedal steel. It plays like a long summer drive record, patient and glowing rather than showy.
lineage: Expands on the debut's Gram Parsons/Grateful Dead-indebted template with a fuller studio sound.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: A patient, groove-heavy record that leans further into the band's live-jam reputation, with extended guitar and pedal-steel interplay over motorik rhythms. Fan reviews compare it to 'Wooden Shjips trading their sails for a prairie schooner' -- psychedelic country rock for a long, stoned drive.
lineage: Continues Johnson's arc from Wooden Shjips' drone-rock toward fully-formed cosmic country.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: A tighter, hookier set than its predecessors, with standout single 'Mariposa' drawing praise from fans as an instant favorite. The band's core lineup (Johnson, Walker, Hasenberg, Jeffery) sound fully locked in, balancing sunlit pop songcraft with room to stretch out.
lineage: Part of Rose City Band's steady evolution of the Gram Parsons/Grateful Dead cosmic-country template into a signature sound.

label: Thrill Jockey
description: Johnson's most emotionally shadowed Rose City Band record to date, letting a melancholy undertone sit alongside the band's usual sun-kissed grooves. Sanae Yamada (Moon Duo) guests on synths and vocals; Barry Walker's pedal steel remains the record's glinting through-line.
lineage: The latest chapter in Johnson's long arc from Wooden Shjips/Moon Duo psych-drone to widescreen cosmic country.

label: Spiritual Pajamas
description: Clay Finch and Sam Blasucci's duo debut is built on intertwined nylon and steel-string acoustic guitars and close, easy harmonies, closer to Everly Brothers or Simon & Garfunkel than jam-band sprawl. It is unhurried, warm California folk-country, intimate rather than expansive.
lineage: Rooted in Laurel Canyon duo harmony singing and 1970s California country rock, feeding directly into the Beachwood Sparks-adjacent scene that includes Silver Synthetic and Farmer Dave Scher.

label: Yep Roc Records
description: The duo's major-imprint debut sharpens the songwriting while keeping the same easygoing intertwined-guitar sound, drawing overt inspiration from the Flying Burrito Brothers and classic California country rock. It is warmer and more fully arranged than their debut, without losing its front-porch intimacy.
lineage: Continues Mapache's Laurel Canyon-via-California-country lineage with a bigger studio budget and outside collaborators.

label: Innovative Leisure / Calico Discos
description: Mapache's third album keeps refining their duo-guitar-and-harmony formula, drawing comparisons to Allah-Las and other West Coast revivalists. It is short, warm and unpretentious, songs built for a porch or a campfire rather than a festival stage.
lineage: A continuation of Mapache's steady development of the California cosmic-country duo sound.

label: Innovative Leisure / Calico Discos
description: An 18-song, hour-long set of earnest, classic songwriting named for the band's dog, with covers of 'Love Can't Hold Me' and 'Light My Fire' folded into the sprawl. As Josh Terry noted, it is an unpretentious road-trip record from a duo comfortable with letting songs breathe.
lineage: The most expansive entry in Mapache's catalog, extending their duo-harmony format across a double-LP-length set.

label: Innovative Leisure / Calico Discos
description: A relaxed, well-loved set that includes a cover of the Flying Burrito Brothers' 'Hot Burrito No. 2' alongside originals like 'French Kiss', continuing the duo's front-porch harmony sound with a slightly fuller band arrangement.
lineage: Extends Mapache's ongoing homage to Flying Burrito Brothers-style California country rock.

label: Scissor Tail / Spinster
description: Rosali Middleman's early solo record pairs plainspoken, deceptively simple songwriting with restrained electric-guitar backing, patient rather than showy. It sets the template for her later work with David Nance's Mowed Sound band: songs that unravel slowly, revealing more with repeat listens.
lineage: Rooted in the Philadelphia DIY folk scene, laying groundwork for her later collaborations with Nebraska's Mowed Sound band on No Medium and Bite Down.

label: Spinster Records
description: Rosali's first collaboration with David Nance's Mowed Sound band opens up her songs into looser, more guitar-forward arrangements, closer to Neil Young or Yo La Tengo than singer-songwriter folk. Josh Terry called it a standout of the decade.
lineage: Marks the start of her ongoing partnership with the Mowed Sound band, a key thread connecting Philadelphia and Omaha DIY scenes.

label: Merge Records
description: Rosali's fourth album and Merge Records debut, again with Nance's Mowed Sound band, elaborates elliptical folk songs into full-bodied guitar rock reminiscent of Yo La Tengo or Neil Young, while her voice carries the mesmerizing pull of Sandy Denny or Will Oldham.
lineage: The full flowering of her Mowed Sound collaboration, moving her from DIY folk circles onto a larger indie label.

label: Self-released
description: Chris Lyons of garage-punk band Bottomfeeders steps into '70s classic-rock territory here, all chiming guitars, T-Rex stomp and Lou Reed-style breeziness. The band favors warmth and laid-back groove over polish, evoking the LP's late-'60s/early-'70s golden era rather than throwback pastiche.
lineage: Grew out of New Orleans garage-punk band Bottomfeeders, redirecting toward Britfolk- and glam-inflected classic rock; connected to the Beachwood Sparks-adjacent Curation Records scene via later releases.

label: Mare Records
description: Kazar's debut solo album, made after years as a sideman for Jeff Tweedy and Steve Gunn, is joyful, unhurried rock built on winding jams and pedal steel from James Elkington. Kevin Morby (Mare Records) compared it to 'David Bowie meets the Band.'
lineage: Grew out of Kazar's years as a touring/session player in the Chicago scene (Wilco, Steve Gunn), released on Kevin Morby's Mare Records imprint.

label: Congrats Records
description: Kazar's second solo LP, produced by Sam Evian, is cozy, conversational folk-rock in a New Morning/Wings register, with Dorian Gehring's pedal steel and fiddle threading through warm, unhurried songs about everyday intimacy.
lineage: Continues Kazar's post-Due North songwriting, deepening ties to the Sam Evian/Flying Cloud studio network shared with Liz Cooper and other C6 artists.

label: Self-released
description: Sean Thompson's first solo EP after years as a Nashville sideman, short and direct, exploring his own songwriting voice with a small backing band of drums, keys and bass. A modest but confident opening statement for the project.
lineage: Grew out of Thompson's time in Nashville DIY bands (Gnarwhal, Promised Land Sound) before he became a touring guitarist for Margo Price and others.

label: Self-released
description: An instrumental trio of Nashville sidemen (Spencer Cullum on pedal steel, Sean Thompson on guitar, Rich Ruth's Michael Ruth on synths) built this debut from a European tour's worth of long-drive jamming. It luxuriates in kosmische, ambient and jazz-fusion textures rather than song structure -- Dead-adjacent in spirit, closer to Alice Coltrane or Ashra in execution.
lineage: Formed from the overlapping session circles of Nashville's Promised Land Sound/Erin Rae/Margo Price world; a spinoff project of Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection and Sean Thompson's Weird Ears.

label: Full Time Hobby
description: The concluding album in pedal-steel player Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection trilogy, made from reel-to-reel field recordings and rough studio takes and built around English folklore. Featuring Erin Rae, Sean Thompson, Rich Ruth and others from his Nashville circle, it is a kaleidoscopic mix of folk, jazz and pop.
lineage: A member of Miranda Lambert's band and pedal-steel player for Angel Olsen, Lambchop and others, Cullum's solo trilogy pulls his Nashville session network into an English folk-rock frame.

label: Sacred Bones Records
description: Cogan's debut for Sacred Bones mixes haunted folk, psych rock and a shadowy strain of country, recorded partly with the country and experimental musicians of her Nanaimo, B.C. circle. Matt Kelly's pedal steel and Patrick M'Gonigle's mandolin ground the record's smoky, '70s-inflected atmosphere.
lineage: A shift for Cogan from her earlier dream-folk/goth-folk records toward explicit country and psych-rock textures, aligning her with the wider cosmic-country revival.

label: Self-released
description: Sam Cantor's Chicago band mixes alt-country songwriting with adventurous, Dead-like guitar theatrics and Max Subar's pedal steel, backed by a rotating cast of Chicago players including Sima Cunningham and Macie Stewart. Josh Terry, who wrote the album's bio, called it his favorite Chicago band's best work.
lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY web as Liam Kazar and Spencer Radcliffe, drawing on Grateful Dead and Crazy Horse guitar lineage filtered through Midwestern alt-country songwriting.

label: Spoilsport Records / Earth Libraries
description: Dylan Young's second Way Dynamic album studies mellow '70s songwriting in the Carole King, Jackson Browne, Harry Nilsson and Todd Rundgren mode, dressed in baroque-pop string arrangements. It is playful and melodic rather than jam-heavy, closer to chamber-pop revivalism than Dead-style sprawl.
lineage: Grows out of Young's work in Melbourne bands Cool Sounds and Good Morning, channeling '70s Laurel Canyon songcraft into a minimalist folk-pop frame.

label: Self-released
description: Way Dynamic's third album continues Dylan Young's painstaking attention to '70s-styled folk-rock harmonies and drum sounds, mixing sincere songwriting with oddball funk detours. Waxahatchee's Katie Crutchfield has singled out the song 'Miffed It' as a favorite.
lineage: Continues Young's Melbourne chamber-pop lineage established on Duck and So Familiar.

label: Self-released
description: Gabe Birnbaum cedes lead vocals throughout to a guest cast (Mutual Benefit's Jordan Lee, V.V. Lightbody, Adam Duritz) over extended, guitar-forward jams and replayable choruses. It is a generous, collaborative record built for a full band stretching out live.
lineage: Birnbaum's main outlet outside his solo work, rooted in the New York DIY/session network that also includes Robber Robber and Sam Evian collaborators.

album: The Congress of Teddy and The Rough Riders
label: Self-released
description: A Dead-inspired, psychedelic-twang debut from a four-piece Nashville band including pedal steel player Luke Schneider, mixing rowdy garage energy with guitar interplay. Recorded at Sam Phillips Recording and mixed by Matt Ross-Spang, it has the loose, live-in-the-room feel of a band raised on both punk and country.
lineage: Part of the same Nashville DIY-country scene as Promised Land Sound and Erin Rae, with member Luke Schneider going on to play pedal steel widely across the C6 lane.

label: Self-released
description: Mapache's Sam Blasucci steps out solo, trading intertwined acoustic guitars for a piano his bandmate's mother gave away, writing fully autobiographical songs about settling into adult life. Covers of Dido's 'Thank You' and the Cranberries' 'Linger' sit unironically alongside the originals.
lineage: A solo detour from Mapache's California cosmic-country duo sound, recorded with Mapache collaborator Johnny Payne at Dan Horne's Lone Palm Studio.

label: Self-released
description: Blasucci's third solo LP, an airy, piano-led set that trades some of Off My Stars' folk directness for a more sophisticated pop croon, with contributions from Andres Renteria, Mia Wilson and Laena Myers. Tasteful rather than showy, it continues his move away from Mapache's guitar-forward sound.
lineage: Follows Off My Stars and the glam-pop Real Life Thing in Blasucci's ongoing solo evolution away from Mapache's duo format.

album: Flight of the Long Distance Healer
label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
description: James Wallace's kaleidoscopic project mixes piano-led psychedelic rock with dense, spacey arrangements and guest turns from Erin Rae, Vetiver and Spencer Cullum. Opaque, mystic lyrics (voiced partly through Wallace's Dr. James Oliver CYR persona) sit over swampy, soulful production.
lineage: Wallace also plays drums in The Dead Tongues and has worked widely across the Nashville/Asheville cosmic-country circle; this album connects Oakland psych with that Southern network via its many guest features.

label: Kill Rock Stars
description: Davis's classically-trained harp anchors a full-band record made with longtime collaborators, weaving 60s pop melodies, psychedelia and driving folk rock. Fans compare it to Fleetwood Mac at their most collaborative; steel guitarist Kurt Johnson gives it a country-rock backbone.
lineage: Davis has shared stages with Bob Weir, Phil Lesh and Circles Around the Sun, and this record leans into that Dead-adjacent, harmony-driven jam-pop lineage.

label: Kill Rock Stars
description: A 'canyon country' record written in a Chevy Chase Canyon hillside home, tying a neo-western future to Laurel Canyon's lineage and the mythos of Elvis's Graceland. It balances light and dark more explicitly than her earlier records while keeping her harp and full-band folk-rock sound intact.
lineage: Continues Davis's arc from harp-led chamber pop toward explicit Laurel Canyon/cosmic-country songwriting.

label: Psychic Hotline
description: Gustafson's fourth and most emotionally direct Dead Tongues album, reckoning with failed relationships and a religious upbringing over full-band arrangements including Molly Sarle and Amelia Meath (Mountain Man/Sylvan Esso) on backing vocals. A statement of, in his words, 'radical acceptance.'
lineage: Deepens Gustafson's connections across the Asheville/Durham folk-rock scene (Mountain Man, Hiss Golden Messenger collaborators).

label: Dead Oceans
description: Walker's breakthrough backs his fingerpicked-guitar songwriting with Chicago jazz and experimental players (including cellist/improviser Fred Lonberg-Holm), stretching folk songs into loose, Van Morrison-and-Tim Buckley-indebted jams. It is warm, exploratory and unhurried.
lineage: Grew out of Walker's Chicago DIY cassette-EP years, pulling jazz improvisation into a folk-rock frame indebted to Astral Weeks and the Grateful Dead's more pastoral side.

album: Golden Sings That Have Been Sung
label: Dead Oceans
description: A deliberate evolution from Primrose Green's jazz-folk sprawl toward tighter, more song-focused arrangements, still built on Walker's intricate guitar work and a loose, breezy band feel. Reviewers noted it as 'yet another change' in his continually shifting sound.
lineage: The second of Walker's Dead Oceans albums, part of his restless movement between folk, jazz and rock idioms.

label: Tompkins Square
description: Burton's debut LP, produced by Jarvis Taveniere of Woods, pairs a high, Roy Orbison-like wail with moody, echo-laden country-rock production. The L.A. Times called it 'an old, weird Americana sound filled with echo and longing' -- timeless rather than retro.
lineage: Produced by Woods' Jarvis Taveniere, tying Burton directly into the Woodsist/cosmic-country lineage; released on Tompkins Square, the American Primitive-adjacent folk label.

label: Matador Records
description: Vile's fifth album stretches sun-baked slacker rock into sprawling, double-LP length, blending gorgeous fingerpicking with heavy guitar drift. The mood is unhurried and half-stoned, closer to a daydream than a statement. It is the record where his Pavement/Crazy Horse-indebted sound became widescreen.
lineage: Descends directly from Pavement's loose-limbed guitar rock and Neil Young's amp-drone side, filtered through Vile's own Philadelphia lo-fi scene alongside The War on Drugs.

label: Matador Records
description: A more introspective, home-recorded turn with banjo and piano alongside the guitars, its lead single 'Pretty Pimpin' became his biggest hit. Vile's cracked, mumbling delivery and stream-of-consciousness lyrics stay pure slacker even as the arrangements soften toward folk.
lineage: Extends the Pavement-to-Silver Jews thread of deadpan funny-sad songwriting into a more folk-inflected register.

label: Domino Recording Company
description: Alex Giannascoli's ninth album pairs pitched-up vocal tics and Auto-Tune warps with plainspoken, sometimes menacing songwriting about faith and small-town life. Josh Terry calls him an essential artist whose imitators only ever capture his gentleness or his menace, never both; 'Runner' is his favorite Alex G song.
lineage: Grew out of Bandcamp-era home recording (indebted to GBV's fragment-song lo-fi) into one of the most imitated songwriters in the current jangle/slacker underground.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Matt Scottoline's project turns plainspoken heartbreak into tight, hook-forward power pop, ten songs recorded with an easy, unfussy jangle. It sits alongside 2nd Grade and Golden Apples in Philly's power-pop revival.
lineage: Big Star and Superchunk by way of the Philadelphia DIY scene that also produced Hop Along and Mo Troper's touring circle.

label: Self-released
description: Russell Edling's group deconstructs its own songwriting process across a spacious, nervy set of fuzzed and jangling power pop, Elephant 6-indebted per Terry, with dreamy mellotron cutting against scrubby guitars.
lineage: Big Star/Elephant 6 melodicism filtered through Philadelphia's current power-pop scene alongside Hurry and 2nd Grade.
key_tracks: Another Grand Offering for the Swine

label: Matador Records
description: Three Chicago teenagers' debut, recorded with John Agnello (Kurt Vile, Dinosaur Jr.), is an efficient romp through indie rock's post-punk and jangle fringes -- Terry says he'd never seen better taste in a young band.
lineage: Draws on Pavement and Sonic Youth's guitar interplay via Chicago's all-ages DIY scene.

label: Matador Records
description: A more direct sophomore set per Terry: ramshackle, perfect pop songs with grooves and glowing harmonies replacing the debut's noisier fringes.
lineage: Continues Horsegirl's Pavement/post-punk lineage toward cleaner pop songwriting.

label: Self-released
description: 16 scrap-rock sketches of telecaster-driven hooks and guitar charm; Terry calls Joe Glass's earworm rippers a mix of Nuggets garage and '90s indie jangle with punk swagger.
lineage: Garage/Nuggets and '90s indie jangle filtered through the Midwest DIY circuit around Good Flying Birds and Sharp Pins.

label: Self-released
description: Adventurous, stylistically shifting indie rock that Terry says still flows front to back, with Built to Spill and Pavement echoes running through eleven tracks.
lineage: Pavement's loose song-suite structure and Built to Spill's guitar interplay.

label: Rotten Apple
description: A twee-punk-leaning collection of home recordings from 2020-2024, re-released on vinyl by Carpark and Smoking Room after underground buzz; Terry hears pristine, thoughtful jangle-pop with GBV-grade hooks and surging punk energy.
lineage: Guided by Voices and Beat Happening's DIY-jangle lineage, shared with tourmates Sharp Pins and Horsegirl.

label: ANTI-
description: Detroit's Bonny Doon make their ANTI- debut breezier and more accessible than past records, per Terry, with lyrics that sneak up on the listener over unhurried, conversational arrangements.
lineage: Slacker-folk in the Silver Jews/Palace mold, filtered through Detroit's indie scene.

label: Grand Jury Music
description: Charlie Martin and Will Taylor's duo makes soft-focus, mid-fi slacker pop, warm and unhurried, built on plain-spoken affection and gentle drum-machine pulses.
lineage: Descends from the lo-fi/DIY college-radio-to-Bandcamp lineage of Duster and Alex G.

label: Arts & Crafts
description: A 19-track double LP that per Terry has stronger melodies and more hi-fi recording than earlier Hovvdy work, praised by Zach Bryan and boygenius.
lineage: Continues Hovvdy's lo-fi slacker-pop arc toward fuller production.

label: Third Man Records
description: Will Anderson's project buries plainspoken, slacker-jangly songwriting under warm shoegaze fuzz; Cartwheel was his Third Man Records debut.
lineage: Sits between countrygaze/shoegaze fuzz and the jangle-pop tradition, indebted to Guided by Voices' song-fragment economy.

label: Seasick Records
description: Loud, relentlessly hooky rock that Terry says channels Summerteeth-era Wilco and Ty Segall's frantic energy, cut live-in-two-days in Muscle Shoals with his band Meadow Dust.
lineage: Neil Young & Crazy Horse fuzz filtered through Birmingham's DIY scene, with Wilco's Americana-pop as a touchstone.

label: Matador Records
description: Will Toledo's first full-band studio album turns eleven Bandcamp-honed years of bedroom pop into classic-rock-scaled narrative rock, nodding to the Cars, Pavement and Jonathan Richman across a sprawling, self-lacerating song cycle.
lineage: Directly descended from the DIY-network/Bandcamp lineage (Toledo self-released 12 albums before signing to Matador), fused with Pavement's slacker irony.

album: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
label: Milk! Records
description: Barnett's debut is a wry, rambling slacker-rock landmark, its deadpan run-on lyrics detailing house-hunting anxiety ('Depreston') and open-mic dread ('Pedestrian at Best') over loose, twangy guitars.
lineage: A direct heir to Pavement's talky slacker rock and the Australian jangle lineage running through Dick Diver and the Goon Sax.

label: Milk! Records
description: A calmer, more self-produced record that trades some of the wordplay density for spacious, drum-machine-inflected slacker pop.
lineage: Barnett's continuing Pavement-indebted songwriting, softened toward indie-pop.

label: Matador Records
description: The Brisbane trio (including Robert Forster's son Louis) add synths and sheen to their Go-Betweens-descended jangle-pop, its trio of songwriters trading plainspoken, bittersweet verses.
lineage: Direct lineage from the Go-Betweens/Flying Nun jangle-pop tradition, one generation removed via founding member Louis Forster.

label: Sub Pop
description: Toronto's Kiwi Jr. sharpen their Pavement/GBV-descended jangle into a wry, hooky sophomore set; Terry notes they've opened for both bands plus the Walkmen and the Lemonheads.
lineage: Direct Pavement/GBV lineage in sound and touring circles.

label: Sub Pop
description: Kiwi Jr.'s third album adds synths and sheen to their wit-and-melody formula, sardonic Toronto indie rock that Terry calls a mastered combination of humor and hooks, building on the jangle of Cooler Returns and Football Money.
lineage: Continues the band's Pavement/GBV-descended jangle.

album: On the Intricate Inner Workings of the System
label: Sub Pop
description: Welsh trio's third LP and Sub Pop debut is Modern-Lovers-meets-Nuggets garage rock with sarcastic dual vocals and clanging riffs; Terry notes their prior LP made his 2023 year-end list.
lineage: Garage/Nuggets by way of the Jonathan Richman/Modern Lovers deadpan-talky lineage.

label: Self-released
description: A sprawling 47-track second LP of relentlessly catchy, fuzz-wrapped garage pop, per Terry, with great dual-singer chemistry.
lineage: Continues the band's garage/Nuggets lineage at maximalist length.

label: Lame-O Records
description: James Goodson's project crams huge hooks into no-second-wasted power pop -- Terry compares it to Fountains of Wayne played at ear-shattering volume, 12 songs in 26 minutes.
lineage: Big Star/Fountains of Wayne melodicism blown out with fuzz-pedal DIY energy.

label: Carpark Records
description: Elizabeth Stokes writes tight, guitar-heavy songs that read as autobiographical character studies of relationships' aftermaths, an 'incandescent collision of power-pop and skuzz' per the band's own liner text.
lineage: New Zealand jangle-pop lineage (Flying Nun-adjacent) crossed with American power pop.

label: Chapter Music
description: Melbourne band's debut is loose, plainspoken jangle-pop full of local color (Melbourne suburb references, wry deadpan vocals) that helped define the 2010s Australian slacker scene alongside Twerps and the Goon Sax.
lineage: Flying Nun-descended jangle by way of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene.

label: Self-released
description: A tightly-recorded set of plainspoken, jangling Melbourne guitar pop, mixed by Tom Hardisty and mastered by Mikey Young, in the same scene as Dick Diver and the Goon Sax.
lineage: Flying Nun-descended Melbourne jangle-pop scene.

label: Double Double Whammy
description: Thx is Hannah Read's hushed, homespun early full-length as Lomelda, ten short songs of plainspoken lyrics over sparse acoustic and electric guitar, recorded with the DIY intimacy that defines her Silsbee, Texas project. It sits at the quiet, unresolved end of the 2010s Bandcamp folk scene, closer to a diary than a studio record.
lineage: An early document in the hemlock/Little Mazarn/Texas hushed-folk network Read has stayed close to; a direct precursor to the fuller-band M for Empathy and Hannah.

label: Double Double Whammy
description: M for Empathy is Hannah Read's most stripped-down Lomelda record, eleven brief, whispery songs built from silence, half-finished phrases and spare guitar. Read has described it as things said or unsaid finally let out, a record about making peace with her own voice.
lineage: The quietest turn in Lomelda's catalog between the full-band Thx and Hannah, deepening her ties to the Texas/hemlock hushed-folk network.

label: Double Double Whammy
description: Hannah is Read's most fleshed-out Lomelda album to date, fourteen tender, unhurried songs that move between fragile solo passages and warmer full-band arrangements while keeping her plainspoken, diaristic lyrics at the center. It is patient, intimate Texas indie folk built for close listening.
lineage: Widely regarded as Lomelda's breakthrough, consolidating the hushed songwriting of Thx and M for Empathy into a fuller sound shared with labelmates in the Double Double Whammy/hemlock orbit.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Plum is Widowspeak's warmest, most unhurried record, recorded with Sam Evian in the Catskills; Molly Hamilton's honeyed voice sits over dusty, sun-worn guitars and easy tempos that lean further into the band's country and 90s-dream-pop touchstones than the darker Expect the Best before it.
lineage: Follows Expect the Best and precedes The Jacket in Widowspeak's later-career turn toward a twangier, more overtly country-inflected version of their dream-pop sound.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Expect the Best is Widowspeak's heaviest, most nocturnal record, four-piece takes on somber indie rock, dream pop and what the band calls 'cowboy grunge.' Molly Hamilton's melodies stay pretty even as the songs sit in dread and self-doubt, recorded by Kevin McMahon (Swans, Real Estate).
lineage: Follows the duo-recorded All Yours and marks Widowspeak's shift to a full touring band, laying groundwork for the country-tinged twang that deepens on Plum and The Jacket.

label: Captured Tracks
description: The Jacket loosely tracks a fictional band's rise and fall through ten songs of layered guitars, dusty percussion and ambling bass; Widowspeak lean fully into their outlaw-country and slowcore reference points (Neil Young, Cowboy Junkies) while keeping Molly Hamilton's voice front and center.
lineage: The most explicitly twangy Widowspeak record to date, recorded back in New York with Homer Steinweiss and mixed by Chris Coady, extending the country turn begun on Plum.

label: Capitol
description: A Wrecking Crew session guitarist turned solo star, Campbell and producer Al De Lory built the title track (a Jimmy Webb song about a lineman's loneliness) into the high point of countrypolitan orchestration, all shimmering strings, subtle pedal steel, and Campbell's warm, unshowy tenor. It is the clearest bridge between Nashville Sound polish and the pop mainstream, a hit on country and adult-contemporary radio alike. It is for listeners who want to hear how far a steel guitar and a string section could carry a country song into the pop charts.
lineage: A pop-crossover cousin to the Nashville Sound records charted in V26 (Patsy Cline, Jim Reeves), taking the genre's countrypolitan side toward Hollywood session-musician sheen rather than the honky-tonk instrumentation that fed alt-country; its commercial path runs forward to Kenny Rogers and eventually the countrypolitan-adjacent pop-country of the 1990s.

album: Does Fort Worth Ever Cross Your Mind
label: MCA Records
description: Strait's fourth album cemented the neotraditionalist swing back to honky-tonk fiddle and steel after a decade of countrypolitan crossover, with his understated Texas baritone delivering the title-track ballad and dancehall shuffles like 'Let's Fall to Pieces Together.' It is plainspoken, ranch-and-dancehall country built for two-stepping, not radio gloss. It matters as the template that a generation of 1980s-90s mainstream country singers, and eventually the entire commercial format, measured itself against.
lineage: A direct reaction against the countrypolitan pop-country of the 1970s (the Glen Campbell/Charlie Rich side of this lane's parent V26), pulling the mainstream back toward honky-tonk instrumentation; Strait's steady commercial dominance set the template Randy Travis, Alan Jackson, and later Luke Combs followed.
key_tracks: Does Fort Worth Ever Cross Your Mind

label: Warner Bros. Nashville
description: Travis's debut, cut with a stripped-down honky-tonk band and his deep, unadorned baritone, arrived as country radio's answer to the countrypolitan glut, full of plainspoken heartbreak songs like '1982' and 'On the Other Hand.' Its multi-platinum success proved there was a mainstream audience hungry for a return to traditional instrumentation and vocal restraint. It is for anyone who wants the sound that reopened Nashville's door to fiddle and steel in the mid-1980s.
lineage: Part of the same mid-1980s neotraditionalist wave as George Strait, pushing the mainstream back toward honky-tonk instrumentation after a countrypolitan-dominated decade; its commercial template runs forward through Alan Jackson and Garth Brooks into 1990s mainstream country.

label: Capitol Nashville
description: Brooks's second album turned country into a stadium format, pairing honky-tonk fiddle with arena-rock dynamics and showmanship on 'Friends in Low Places' and 'The Thunder Rolls.' Its scale of sales (diamond-certified) rewired what a country album could be commercially. It is for listeners who want the moment country music started selling like classic rock.
lineage: Grows out of the neotraditionalist instrumentation Strait and Travis reestablished, but redirects it toward arena-scale showmanship and crossover pop production, opening the commercial path that leads to 1990s superstar country and eventually bro-country's stadium ambitions.

label: Arista Nashville
description: Jackson's second album kept the neotraditionalist commitment to fiddle and steel alive inside the increasingly pop-leaning mainstream, the title track a wry honky-tonk defense of traditional country against the era's pop-crossover pressure. His plain-spoken Georgia drawl and unfussy arrangements made him the genre's steadiest traditionalist even as the format modernized around him. It is for anyone who wants the last gasp of pure honky-tonk instrumentation inside 1990s Music Row.
lineage: A direct continuation of the Strait/Travis neotraditionalist lane, explicitly defending 'a little bit of Hank' against pop-country encroachment even as the format moved toward the Garth Brooks arena model.

label: Mercury Records
description: Produced with then-husband Mutt Lange, Come On Over fused country storytelling with arena-pop and rock production (programmed drums, big guitar hooks) on hits like 'Man! I Feel Like a Woman!' and 'You're Still the One,' becoming the best-selling country album by a woman ever. It sanded away nearly all twang for maximal pop crossover appeal. It is for listeners tracing how far countrypolitan's pop instincts could travel before the genre line disappeared.
lineage: Takes the pop-crossover ambitions of the countrypolitan lane (Glen Campbell, and later Garth Brooks's arena scale) to their commercial extreme, largely abandoning traditional instrumentation; its pop-first template anticipates the vocal-hook-driven side of 2010s mainstream country.
key_tracks: Man! I Feel Like a Woman!

label: Republic Nashville
description: Built around the inescapable 'Cruise,' the duo's debut fused trap-adjacent beats, party-anthem lyrics about trucks and tailgates, and rap-influenced vocal cadences into what critics quickly labeled bro-country. It is glossy, hook-first, and built for a truck stereo rather than a dancehall. It is for tracing exactly where mainstream country's honky-tonk instrumentation gave way to hip-hop-inflected pop production.
lineage: Descends from the arena-scale, pop-crossover ambitions of Garth Brooks and Shania Twain, but replaces steel guitar and fiddle almost entirely with programmed beats and rap cadence; alongside Jason Aldean's 'Dirt Road Anthem,' it opens the bro-country era that Luke Bryan and eventually Morgan Wallen would inherit.

label: Broken Bow Records
description: Aldean's fourth album broke bro-country wide with 'Dirt Road Anthem,' a Colt Ford-cowritten track sung in a half-rapped cadence over a hip-hop-indebted beat, alongside more traditional rockers like 'My Kinda Party.' The mix of country subject matter (trucks, dirt roads, small towns) with rap-inflected delivery previewed the genre's next decade. It is for hearing the exact single that made country-rap commercially unavoidable.
lineage: A key hinge point between 2000s arena country and full bro-country, taking Southern rock's guitar muscle and grafting on rap cadence and hip-hop production; it directly set up Florida Georgia Line's 2012 breakthrough and the genre wave that followed.

label: Big Loud/Republic
description: A sprawling 30-song double album mixing bro-country hooks, hip-hop-adjacent production, and hard-country balladry, Dangerous became the best-selling album (of any genre) of 2021 in the US, propelled by Wallen's rasping East Tennessee drawl. It is loud, maximalist mainstream country built to dominate streaming as much as radio. It is for hearing where bro-country's commercial machinery had arrived a decade after Florida Georgia Line's debut.
lineage: The commercial endpoint of the bro-country lineage running from Jason Aldean and Florida Georgia Line, now scaled to streaming-era volume and genre-blending with hip-hop and pop; Luke Combs runs parallel to Wallen as the more traditionalist mainstream-country pole of the same moment.

label: River House Artists/Columbia Nashville
description: Combs's debut kept bro-country's blue-collar, beer-and-truck subject matter but sang it in a big, classic-rock-scaled baritone with more guitar muscle and less programmed beat than the Florida Georgia Line generation, on hits like 'Hurricane' and the title track. It became one of the longest-charting albums in Billboard 200 history. It is for the mainstream-country audience that wanted arena size without fully leaving guitar-band instrumentation behind.
lineage: A traditionalist correction inside the bro-country era, pulling the commercial mainstream back toward guitar-driven arrangements even while keeping bro-country's blue-collar, party-and-heartbreak subject matter; runs parallel to Morgan Wallen as the two dominant male mainstream-country stars of the later 2010s.

label: BBR Music Group
description: Produced by Jay Joyce, Wilson's breakthrough mixes 1970s-leaning steel guitar and rock riffs with unconventional production choices (fuzzed guitars, odd textures) under her thick Louisiana drawl, on songs like 'Heart Like a Truck.' It sold mainstream country as a persona ('bell bottom country') rather than just a sound, winning CMA and ACM top honors. It is for listeners who want current mainstream country with more rock grit than Music Row's usual polish.
lineage: A 2020s continuation of the mainstream-country lineage running through Combs and Wallen, but with Jay Joyce's rock-leaning production pulling it closer to the Southern-rock-inflected edge of the format.

label: Atlantic/Assemble Sound
description: A seven-song EP of atmospheric, hypnotic mainstream country about economic anxiety and small-town Georgia life, sung in Avalon's plainspoken drawl over spare, moody production. It is quieter and more downcast than the genre's usual party mode. It is for listeners watching for the next Nashville crossover artist in the Kacey Musgraves mold.
lineage: A newer, more atmospheric strand of the mainstream-Nashville lineage, closer in mood to Kacey Musgraves's pop-leaning country turn than to bro-country's party anthems, suggesting a possible future branch away from the Wallen/Combs commercial center.

label: Universal South
description: The Oklahoma band's major-label debut is loud, guitar-forward Red Dirt rock, closer to Southern rock and outlaw country than to Nashville polish, built for college-town bar shows across Texas and Oklahoma. Cody Canada's raspy drawl and the band's road-tested live-band chemistry made them the flagship act of the Red Dirt scene's crossover moment. It is for hearing the Stillwater/Oklahoma State University bar circuit that fed the 2000s Texas-country boom.
lineage: Grows out of the same outlaw-country and Southern-rock lineages (V24 Texas songwriter tradition, V23/V7 rock) but stays a self-contained regional scene rather than crossing fully into indie or alt-country; its live-circuit model fed directly into Turnpike Troubadours and the wider Red Dirt scene of the 2000s-2010s.

label: Universal/Republic
description: Green's major-label breakthrough is the moment the independent Texas-country dancehall circuit crossed over into the Nashville mainstream, the gold-certified title track landing on national country radio. It is glossier and more radio-built than his earlier, scrappier records, but keeps the Texas-scene sensibility of communal, singalong choruses. It is for tracing how the Texas country scene's stars started migrating toward major-label arena country.
lineage: Bridges the independent Texas-country/dancehall scene (the Robert Earl Keen/Pat Green college-circuit tradition documented in V13/V24) with the Nashville mainstream, previewing how Red Dirt and Texas-country artists would later cross into arena Americana via Stapleton and Zach Bryan.
key_tracks: Tell Me Something I Don't Know

label: Bossier City Records
description: The album that made the Turnpike Troubadours the defining band of the 2010s Red Dirt scene, its fiddle-and-guitar arrangements framing Evan Felker's novelistic character songs ('Diamonds & Gasoline,' '7 & 7') about small-town Oklahoma life. It is more literary than most Red Dirt records, closer to Robert Earl Keen's storytelling than to Southern-rock riffing. It is for listeners who want Red Dirt's biggest 2010s crossover success before Zach Bryan's streaming-era version of the same regional pride.
lineage: The band that carried the Cross Canadian Ragweed/Jason Boland generation's Red Dirt scene into the 2010s festival circuit, with storytelling closer to the Guy Clark/Robert Earl Keen Texas songwriter tradition; its audience overlaps directly with the arena-scale Americana of Stapleton and Bryan that followed.

label: Mercury Nashville
description: After years as a Nashville songwriter, Stapleton's solo debut (produced with Dave Cobb) paired old-school Southern-rock and soul instrumentation with his enormous, gravel-and-smoke voice, most famously on the ubiquitous cover 'Tennessee Whiskey.' Its surprise CMA sweep reoriented mainstream country's taste toward rootsier, less radio-slick production for the rest of the decade. It is for anyone tracing how arena-scale Americana became commercially viable inside the country mainstream.
lineage: Draws on the Southern-rock and outlaw-country lineages (V7, V23) filtered through Dave Cobb's rootsier Nashville production, opening the commercial lane that Zach Bryan and the arena-Americana wave of the later 2010s-2020s would scale even further.

label: Warner Records
description: A sprawling 34-song set that turned Bryan's earnest, unpolished songwriting (equal parts military-brat plainspokenness and diary-entry directness) into a streaming-era phenomenon, melodic and frank in ways that made its simplicity an asset rather than a limitation. It arrived with almost none of Nashville's studio machinery behind it, built instead on volume of songs and a devoted online fanbase. It is for hearing how a self-recorded, DIY-adjacent country songwriter became arena-scale without going through the mainstream Nashville pipeline.
lineage: Emerges from the same Oklahoma singer-songwriter and Red Dirt-adjacent tradition as Turnpike Troubadours but scales it to streaming-era volume and a rougher, unpolished delivery closer to lo-fi singer-songwriter records than to full-band Red Dirt; its runaway popularity opened the commercial lane for Wyatt Flores and other young Oklahoma/Texas songwriters.

label: Warner Records
description: Bryan's self-titled fourth album topped the Billboard 200 on the strength of 'I Remember Everything' (a duet with Kacey Musgraves), tightening the songwriting from American Heartbreak's sprawl while keeping the same unpolished, diaristic delivery. It is quieter and more focused than its predecessor even as its commercial reach grew larger. It is for hearing the record that made Bryan a genuine arena headliner.
lineage: A direct continuation of American Heartbreak's plainspoken, streaming-first songwriting, further cementing Bryan as the commercial center of the arena-Americana wave alongside Stapleton.

label: OEG/Island
description: An Oklahoma State University-scene songwriter whose plainspoken acoustic songs about heartbreak and hometown drift follow directly in Zach Bryan's commercial and stylistic wake, with a rawer, less arena-scaled vocal delivery. It stayed close to the Stillwater/Red Dirt bar circuit even as streaming numbers grew fast. It is for hearing the next generation of Oklahoma singer-songwriters emerging behind Bryan's breakthrough.
lineage: A direct stylistic descendant of Zach Bryan, working the same Stillwater, Oklahoma Red Dirt-adjacent singer-songwriter lane at a smaller scale, suggesting the arena-Americana boom's commercial pipeline continuing into a new generation.

label: Warner Music Nashville/CoJo Music
description: Johnson's second major-label album followed years of independent success on the Texas dancehall circuit, keeping fiddle-and-steel instrumentation and rodeo-circuit authenticity intact even as the record's scale (30 songs, double-album format) matched arena-country ambitions. His booming baritone carries both barroom rockers and gospel-tinged ballads. It is for hearing a Texas-country independent star's path into the Nashville mainstream without abandoning traditional instrumentation.
lineage: Follows the same Texas-country-to-mainstream trajectory Pat Green traveled two decades earlier, but arrives with the fiddle-and-steel instrumentation intact, closer to the neotraditionalist wing of mainstream country than to bro-country's programmed beats.

label: Nettwerk
description: Produced by David Rawlings, the string band's national debut fuses old-time and bluegrass instrumentation with punk-scaled energy, most famously on 'Wagon Wheel' (built from a Bob Dylan chorus fragment by frontman Ketch Secor), which became one of the most-covered songs of the 2000s. It is rowdier and more raucous than traditional old-time music, aimed at festival crowds rather than folk-revival purists. It is for hearing the record that helped launch the festival-scale Americana boom of the 2000s-2010s.
lineage: Bridges old-time and bluegrass tradition (this lane's X4 parent) with a punk-energy, festival-scaled string-band sound; 'Wagon Wheel' became a foundational singalong for the entire stomp-clap-folk wave that the Avett Brothers and Mumford & Sons scaled to arenas.

label: American Recordings
description: Produced by Rick Rubin, the Avetts' major-label debut smoothed their earlier punk-folk roughness into fuller, string-and-piano-arranged Americana, the title track and 'January Wedding' built for big emotional payoffs and festival-crowd singalongs. It kept their brothers' close harmonies and confessional lyrics but scaled the sound to arenas. It is for hearing the moment stomp-clap folk pivoted from underground string-band roughness to mainstream festival Americana.
lineage: Grows out of the Avetts' earlier punk-folk-adjacent scrappiness (their own path runs back toward folk-punk and old-time string-band tradition) but this album redirects it toward the festival-scale Americana mainstream that Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers would soon dominate commercially.

label: Island Records/Glassnote Records
description: The London band's debut defined the stomp-clap-folk sound proper: banjo strum building to shouted group choruses, quiet-to-loud dynamics borrowed as much from indie rock as from folk revival, on hits like 'Little Lion Man' and 'The Cave.' It is unapologetically anthemic, built for festival main stages rather than folk clubs. It is for hearing the single most influential template of the 2010s festival-folk boom.
lineage: Takes the festival-Americana energy Old Crow Medicine Show and the Avett Brothers had been building in the US and turns it into a globally exportable UK indie-folk formula, directly inspiring the Lumineers and the entire stomp-clap-folk wave of the early 2010s.

label: Dualtone
description: The band's self-titled debut, driven by the singalong stomp-clap of 'Ho Hey,' distilled the Mumford & Sons formula into a leaner, more American-radio-friendly package: acoustic guitar, cello, minimal percussion, and audience-participation hooks. It became a top-five, multi-platinum crossover hit. It is for hearing stomp-clap folk at its most streamlined and commercially dominant.
lineage: A direct American response to Mumford & Sons' UK folk-revival formula, stripping it down further for pop radio; alongside the Avett Brothers, it defined the festival-Americana mainstream that Brandi Carlile and the Head and the Heart would extend through the 2010s.

label: Sub Pop
description: Originally self-released and sold at Seattle shows before Sub Pop picked it up, the band's debut leans on three-part harmonies, piano and violin melodies, and steady, festival-ready percussion on songs like 'Rivers and Roads.' It is warmer and more communal than Mumford & Sons' bombast, closer to campfire harmony singing scaled up. It is for hearing the softer, more indie-rock-adjacent wing of the stomp-clap-folk boom.
lineage: A Pacific Northwest, indie-label (Sub Pop) variant of the same festival-folk wave the Lumineers and Mumford & Sons were riding, closer to indie-pop harmony singing than to old-time string-band roots.

album: By the Way, I Forgive You
label: Low Country Sound/Elektra
description: Produced by Dave Cobb with the Hanseroth twins, Carlile's sixth album fuses big-voiced folk-rock balladry with orchestral strings on 'The Joke' and 'Every Time I Hear That Song,' scaling festival-Americana emotion to Grammy-stage size. It is more vocally virtuosic and personal than the genre's usual crowd-singalong mode. It is for hearing Americana's festival mainstream at its most emotionally direct and critically decorated.
lineage: A more singer-songwriter-driven, less banjo-strum-dependent branch of the same festival-Americana mainstream as the Lumineers and Avett Brothers, closer in vocal scale to 1970s folk-rock than to stomp-clap folk proper.
key_tracks: Every Time I Hear That Song

label: Stax
description: After a career in quieter folk music, Rateliff reinvented himself with a horn section and Stax-style soul-revival energy on 'S.O.B.,' a stomp-and-shout single that became a festival-circuit anthem far bigger than his earlier solo folk records. It swaps banjo strum for horns and gang vocals but keeps the same communal, crowd-participation energy as the rest of this lane. It is for hearing the soul-revival cousin of stomp-clap folk's festival-anthem instinct.
lineage: Shares the same festival-crowd, singalong-anthem instinct as Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers but channels it through horn-driven Stax soul rather than banjo folk, an adjacent branch of the big-tent Americana mainstream.

label: Mulberry Records
description: A Fort Smith-to-Nashville songwriter's swampy, familiar-sounding country rock that draws on Bobby Charles-style Southern groove without feeling derivative, closer to Americana's big-tent song-craft tradition than to Red Dirt's bar-band rowdiness. It is warm, unhurried, and built for the same festival Americana audience as the Avett Brothers or JD Souther's generation of songwriters. It is for hearing where the festival-Americana mainstream and the Southern songwriter tradition currently overlap.
lineage: Sits at the overlap of the big-tent Americana festival scene and the Southern/Texas songwriter tradition, closer to swampy roots-rock songcraft than to stomp-clap folk's banjo-strum anthems.

label: Mercury Nashville/UMG Nashville
description: The husband-and-wife duo's major-label debut mixes soul and gospel vocal power with Americana songwriting, their trading, dueting vocals (Michael and Tanya Trotter) drawing on both Stax soul and festival-Americana's big-emotion instincts. Its crossover into country awards recognition (a first for a Black duo in that format) marked a widening of the genre's commercial mainstream. It is for hearing gospel-soul vocal tradition meeting the big-tent Americana and country-award circuit.
lineage: A gospel-and-soul-rooted branch of the festival-Americana mainstream, sharing the emotional bigness of Brandi Carlile's records and eventually crossing into the arena-Americana/country-award circuit via their Zach Bryan collaboration.

label: Starday Records
description: The debut of the band that coined the term 'newgrass,' fusing traditional bluegrass instrumentation (banjo, mandolin, fiddle) with rock and jazz-influenced improvisation and a hippie-era openness to extended jamming. It broke from bluegrass orthodoxy's strict traditionalism far more aggressively than contemporaries like the Osborne Brothers. It is for hearing bluegrass's founding progressive-jam experiment, decades before Billy Strings.
lineage: Descends directly from the first-generation bluegrass tradition (Bill Monroe, the Stanley Brothers, documented in this lane's parent R1) but breaks from its strict traditionalism to found the 'newgrass' style, opening the improvisational, genre-blending path that Nickel Creek, Punch Brothers, and Billy Strings all eventually walk.

label: Rounder
description: Krauss's crystalline fiddle and vocal purity, paired with Union Station's tight, polished bluegrass picking (Dan Tyminski, Jerry Douglas), made this the crossover-friendly, radio-ready face of modern bluegrass just before O Brother, Where Art Thou? sent the genre briefly mainstream. It is cleaner and more vocally driven than jam-leaning newgrass. It is for hearing bluegrass's most award-decorated, mainstream-crossover-capable ensemble.
lineage: A polished, vocal-forward continuation of the first-generation bluegrass tradition (this lane's parent R1), positioned opposite the jam-leaning newgrass lineage of New Grass Revival and Billy Strings; Krauss's crossover success helped keep bluegrass commercially visible into the 2000s.
key_tracks: Let Me Touch You for a While

label: Sugar Hill
description: Produced by Alison Krauss, the trio's redefining third album (their earlier two are out of print) mixes bluegrass virtuosity (Chris Thile's mandolin, Sara Watkins's fiddle) with pop songcraft and progressive-newgrass instrumental stretches. It introduced bluegrass technique to a younger, indie-adjacent audience far from the genre's traditional base. It is for hearing the record that launched Chris Thile's decades-long push to blend bluegrass virtuosity with art-music ambition.
lineage: A direct newgrass descendant of New Grass Revival's genre-blending example, filtered through pop songcraft; Chris Thile's continued evolution from this record leads straight into Punch Brothers' more art-music-inflected bluegrass.

label: Rounder
description: Strings's second solo album won a Best Bluegrass Album Grammy on the strength of blistering flatpicked guitar runs and jam-band-scaled improvisation layered over traditional bluegrass songwriting, drawing a younger, festival- and jam-scene audience (including a Bob Weir cosign) into bluegrass. It is faster and more rock-adjacent in its soloing than Krauss's polished ensemble sound. It is for hearing bluegrass's 2010s-2020s jam-band crossover moment.
lineage: The clearest 2010s-2020s inheritor of New Grass Revival's improvisational newgrass experiment, scaled to jam-band festival culture; Strings's success opened commercial space for Molly Tuttle and Sierra Ferrell's own genre-blending bluegrass in the same period.

label: Nonesuch
description: Tuttle's first album with her band Golden Highway (and first for Nonesuch) won the Grammy for Best Bluegrass Album, its guest list (Margo Price, Billy Strings, Old Crow Medicine Show, Gillian Welch) mapping the current bluegrass-and-Americana overlap. Co-produced with dobro player Jerry Douglas, it keeps virtuosic flatpicking guitar at its center while writing personally about growing up different in a small bluegrass town. It is for hearing bluegrass's current critical and commercial high point.
lineage: A 2020s culmination of the same newgrass lineage running from New Grass Revival through Nickel Creek, directly collaborating with Billy Strings and Old Crow Medicine Show as peers in the current bluegrass revival.

label: Rounder
description: A West Virginia-to-Nashville songwriter whose sound blends bluegrass and old-time instrumentation with vintage country, gypsy-jazz, and folk textures, Trail of Flowers swept the 2024 Americana Music Awards. Her flexible, old-timey-inflected voice moves between wistful balladry and rowdy string-band numbers without settling into one lane. It is for hearing bluegrass and old-time tradition filtered through a genuinely idiosyncratic, festival-scale voice.
lineage: A genre-blurring newgrass/old-time descendant that shares Molly Tuttle's and Billy Strings's current bluegrass-revival moment while pulling in vintage pop and gypsy-jazz textures closer to X2's arena-Americana crossover audience.

label: ANTI-
description: McCalla's fourth album, sung substantially in Haitian Creole, pairs accomplished clawhammer banjo and cello with a narrative about Radio Haiti and her Haitian-American identity, drawing on old-time string-band technique as a vehicle for a story far from the genre's usual Appalachian frame. It includes a striking Caetano Veloso cover. It is for hearing old-time banjo tradition applied to a Haitian-American, French-Creole songwriting project.
lineage: Uses old-time string-band technique (banjo, in the lineage of this lane's parent R1) as a vehicle for Haitian-American and Creole storytelling, a geographically and culturally distinct branch of the old-time tradition from its Appalachian mainstream.
